core: What a logo is and does: a graphic mark whose job is to identify, not to describe or sell directly
The common logo types: wordmark/logotype, lettermark/monogram, pictorial mark/logomark, abstract mark, mascot, combination mark, emblem
The principles of an effective logo: simple, memorable, timeless/enduring, versatile, appropriate
Practical reproduction requirements: works in a single color, legible at small sizes, reproduces across media
Why professional logos are constructed as vector artwork (named; mechanics handed to the raster-versus-vector topic)
supporting: Paul Rand's criteria for judging a logo (distinctiveness, visibility, useability, memorability, universality, durability, timelessness) and his principle that a logo derives meaning from the quality of what it symbolizes
That a logo is one element of a larger brand identity system (handed to the branding topic)
That 'appropriate' means fit for audience, not a literal picture of the business
outOfScope: The whole brand identity system and brand strategy (own topic: branding)
File-format mechanics and the full raster-versus-vector distinction (own topic: raster-versus-vector)
Typeface categories used in wordmarks (own topic: typeface-classification)
Trademark registration procedure and legal advice

claims.claim: A logo's primary function is to identify an organization, product, or person; Paul Rand argued a logo 'doesn't sell (directly), it identifies' and is rarely a literal description of a business.
A logo takes on meaning through association with what it stands for; Rand stated a logo 'derives its meaning from the quality of the thing it symbolizes, not the other way around.'
Logos are commonly classified into seven families: wordmark (logotype), lettermark (monogram), pictorial mark (logomark/brand mark), abstract mark, mascot, combination mark, and emblem.

A wordmark sets the full business name in a distinctive typeface; a lettermark reduces a long name to its initials; a pictorial mark is a recognizable image; an abstract mark is a non-representational geometric form; a mascot is an illustrated character; a combination mark pairs a symbol with text; and an emblem places the name inside a shape such as a badge, seal, or crest.

Design literature converges on a short checklist of qualities for an effective logo: simple, memorable, timeless/enduring, versatile, and appropriate — a formulation popularized in David Airey's Logo Design Love and grounded in Paul Rand's earlier criteria.

Paul Rand listed the qualities of a good logo as distinctiveness, visibility, useability, memorability, universality, durability, and timelessness, and held that simplicity is difficult to achieve yet worth the effort.
A logo should be attractive, reproducible in one color, and legible at exceedingly small sizes; 'appropriate' means suited to its audience rather than a literal depiction of the business.

Professional logos are built as vector artwork so the same file scales to any size without losing quality, which is why vectors are the standard construction for logos; the raster-versus-vector file mechanics are covered by that topic.
A logo is one element within a larger brand identity system that also includes color, typography, imagery, and voice; the surrounding system is the subject of branding.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The number and names of logo 'types' vary between sources (some list 7, others 9 or 10) and popular usage often equates 'logo' with 'brand'.
positions: Most design references use a core seven-type taxonomy (wordmark, lettermark, pictorial, abstract, mascot, combination, emblem).
Some marketing sites split these further (e.g. separating logotype from wordmark) or add categories like 'dynamic' logos.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the widely shared seven-family taxonomy as a practical vocabulary, notes the boundaries are conventions rather than strict categories, and keeps the whole brand system in the branding topic.

sourceRecords.title: Logos, Flags, and Escutcheons (1991)
sourceRecords.notes: Primary essay by the designer Paul Rand, read via the paulrand.design archive. Supports: a logo's job is to identify (it 'doesn't sell (directly), it identifies') and is rarely a description of a business; 'A logo derives its meaning from the quality of the thing it symbolizes, not the other way around'; the role of simplicity ('Simplicity is difficult to achieve, yet worth the effort'); the seven qualities of a good logo (distinctiveness, visibility, useability, memorability, universality, durability, timelessness); and that a logo should be reproducible in one color and at exceedingly small sizes. REFERENCE_ONLY copyrighted text; only short attributed phrases quoted.

sourceRecords.title: Logo Design Love: A Guide to Creating Iconic Brand Identities
sourceRecords.notes: Widely cited design-literature title (free sample chapter hosted by the author). Supports the popular five-quality checklist for an effective logo (simple, memorable, timeless, versatile, appropriate), the point that appropriateness does not require literal depiction of the business, and that logos should be designed in vector format so they work across media and at any size. REFERENCE_ONLY: facts and the checklist framing used; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 7 Types of Logos and When to Use Them
sourceRecords.notes: Commercial design reference used to corroborate the standard seven-family logo taxonomy and each type's distinguishing feature: wordmark/logotype (full name in distinctive type), lettermark/monogram (initials), pictorial mark/brand mark (recognizable image, 'the symbol has to do all the work'), abstract mark (non-representational geometric shape), mascot (illustrated character), combination mark (symbol plus text, side-by-side/stacked/integrated), emblem (text inside a badge, seal, or crest). REFERENCE_ONLY: taxonomy facts only; example brands named descriptively; no prose reproduced.
